# Internal or external fitting

In an age-based assessment, the production function, and hence the reference points, are largely determined by parameters that are treated as fixed — growth, fecundity, and natural mortality-at-age — and by the steepness of the stock–recruitment relationship [@Mangel2013steepness]. The stock–recruitment relationship may be fitted internally as part of the assessment or post hoc. SSB and recruitment are not observations, however: they are model estimates, and stock-assessment data sets do not always contain enough information to estimate the key parameters [@Lee2011M; @Lee2012steepness]. Observations are seldom complete, and the quantities of interest are latent, so alternative choices can provide equally good fits [@Barlow1972isotonic].

Ideally the stock–recruitment relationship and the reference points should be estimated within the model. That allows a fully integrated analysis in which all sources of data and uncertainty are considered together. If the assessment is an integrated or statistical catch-at-age model, formal diagnostics can be applied [@Carvalho2021cookbook], the sensitivity of stock status relative to the reference points can be evaluated, and uncertainty can be propagated by sampling the values of fixed parameters from pre-specified distributions.

# Why internal estimation

Stock-assessment models include many assumptions. Estimating the stock–recruitment relationship inside the model keeps those estimates consistent with both the assumptions and the model structure. That consistency matters for the reliability of predictions and of the management advice based on them.

Internal estimation also makes it possible to quantify uncertainty more fully: from the data and from the fixed parameters or priors, through the stock–recruitment relationship, to assessment outputs such as biomass and fishing mortality relative to target and limit reference points. Estimating the relationship post hoc can introduce bias and inconsistency by not accounting for the interconnectedness of stock dynamics — for example if process error is modelled as recruitment but is generated by other processes such as natural mortality.

# SAM

Stock–recruitment relationships can also be fitted inside the state-space assessment model (SAM), to explore hypotheses about productivity and to evaluate the implications for biological reference points. That is a data-informed assessment strategy: it recognises the difficulty of modelling stock–recruitment and the need to integrate all sources of data and uncertainty, and to validate empirically using prediction skill.

Estimating the relationship inside the assessment, rather than outside it, is how information gaps and uncertainty propagation should be addressed. Environmental covariates can then be added using a structured approach to model fitting, with diagnostics used to improve the assessment and to keep management advice robust and risk-equivalent — that is, so that risks do not depend on the level of uncertainty. Autocorrelated recruitment, and whether it can be estimated in an integrated model, is part of that same question [@Johnson2016autocorrelated].

SAM supports around 33 stock–recruitment models, covering common, time-series, and depensatory forms, with more easily added. Error models include AR and other temporal structures. Deterministic and stochastic reference points are available, with ongoing work on the stochastic estimates.

# Diagnostics at the benchmark

When the base-case model is developed at a benchmark, a sensitivity analysis should be run for different hypotheses about the functional form of the stock–recruitment relationship (for example Beverton–Holt, Ricker, and Beverton–Holt with and without depensation). Diagnostics should include:

- whether recruitment is driven by SSB or SSB is driven by recruitment, for example Spearman rank cross-correlations [@Szuwalski2015recruitment];
- runs tests for regime shifts and the presence of autocorrelation;
- prediction residuals and MASE for validation [@Kell2021validation].

If those diagnostics do not identify a single best assessment, an ensemble should be used, with the weighting rule agreed in advance. If a post-hoc procedure is used instead, it should at least be verified, for example by simulation testing.

# Procedures, operating models, and metrics

There is also a need for clear definitions: between management procedures and operating models, and between operational reference points and performance metrics. Operational reference points trigger management action in an advice rule — thresholds such as $\mathrm{MSYB}_{\mathrm{trigger}}$. Performance metrics are targets such as $B_{\mathrm{MSY}}$, used to assess whether objectives are met. Methods for estimating probabilities manage impact limits (tails) differently from targets (medians).

# Segmented-regression proxies

Proxy reference points based on segmented regression are a pragmatic choice. Segmented regression may not be biologically plausible, but it can be a practical solution. It should still be simulation-tested, through a systematic check of how model outputs respond to different inputs, so that the proxy operational reference points are shown to be robust. That does not necessarily require MSE. A benchmarked SS3 assessment that already includes a fitted stock–recruitment relationship under a range of hypotheses can be used to evaluate proxies estimated post hoc.

# When external fitting is useful

Fitting a stock–recruitment relationship outside the assessment, using model estimates of SSB and recruits, may still be useful in specific cases. These include assessments that cannot internally accommodate the required complexity, because of the model framework or computational limits, and cases where additional hypotheses need to be explored before they are built into the main assessment — for example the implications of depensation for current advice.

External fitting also allows comparison across stocks, to identify general patterns or effects on the operational reference points used in harvest control rules, without running a full assessment for each case. Restricting the analysis to the SSB–recruitment pair, without the rest of the assessment, can show the range of stock–recruitment dynamics and help choose functional forms for stock-specific assessments. When the assessment is large and computationally expensive, external fits save time in preliminary sensitivity analysis and hypothesis generation — for example exploring auto- and cross-correlation, and the effect of fixed parameters and priors on reference points.

# Conditions for external fitting

The external fit must not introduce assumptions or results that are inconsistent with the main assessment. Any conclusions must take account of how uncertainty in the estimated SSB and recruitment series affects the fitted relationship. As with internal estimation, externally fitted models should be validated and subjected to sensitivity analysis, so that their robustness and the implications for management advice are known.

In short, fitting a stock–recruitment relationship outside the assessment can help with exploratory analysis, comparison across stocks, simplification of complex assessments, and communication. Those analyses still have to be aligned with the objectives and methods of the assessment itself.
